source.title: Mind the Heads: Topological Representation Alignment for Multimodal LLMs
source.authors: Davide Caffagni; Alberto Compagnoni; Federico Melis; Sara Sarto; Pier Luigi Dovesi; Mark Granroth-Wilding; M. Cornia; L. Baraldi

record.tranche_reason: The study uses the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and MKNN alignment to motivate HeRA, a training method for improving MLLMs. Its alignment measurements are outcomes of alignment deliberately induced by HeRA, not tests of whether alignment naturally increases with scale or capability.
record.gate_note: The study applies a contrastive alignment objective to selected attention heads and measures MKNN alignment after training. Because this alignment is induced on purpose, those measurements do not test the natural convergence described by the claim versions; they are recorded under versions ["none"]. VQA and hallucination benchmark results are omitted because they measure task performance, not representation convergence. The PRH correlation cited from prior work is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study uses the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the MKNN metric to motivate and select heads for HeRA, a training objective. Its alignment results come from alignment it induces on purpose, and its headline results are VQA and hallucination benchmarks. It does have a descriptive analysis of natural head and layer MKNN alignment between text-only Qwen2.5 LLMs (3B, 7B, 14B) and DINOv2-L (Fig. 3, 6, 7 left). However, it reports no scale or capability trend, no exact values, and no claim that alignment rises with model quality. So it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, but incomplete. The authors conclude that HeRA, a contrastive proxy for MKNN applied to the least-aligned attention heads, improves MLLMs. The gains are mainly on vision-centric benchmarks (about +0.7 to +3.6), without hurting general, knowledge or OCR tasks, and with reduced hallucinations. They also state that targeting the least-aligned heads beats targeting the top heads, and that this corroborates PRH's alignment–performance correlation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses MKNN as an alignment diagnostic, but changes the intervention: HeRA trains selected attention heads with a contrastive proxy rather than measuring natural alignment convergence across model scale.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment effects depend on which heads are selected: HeRA raises MKNN alignment in the targeted least-aligned heads, while the top-aligned heads remain similar to the LLaVA baseline. The study also compares teacher encoders and head counts for HeRA, but those comparisons do not test natural convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: In text-only Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B, some individual attention heads show far higher natural MKNN alignment with DINOv2-L than any whole layer (Fig. 3, 6, 7 left).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-modal alignment measured at the attention-head level can greatly exceed layer-level alignment within the same LLM, so measured convergence depends on representation granularity.

fits_no_version.finding: The relative head alignment ranking is largely preserved after standard LLaVA training. Multimodal training alone raises top-head alignment; most regularizers mirror the LLaVA baseline (Fig. 5, 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multimodal instruction training raises already-aligned heads' cross-modal MKNN but leaves poorly aligned heads poorly aligned.

fits_no_version.finding: HeRA's contrastive objective raises MKNN of targeted worst-aligned heads by roughly +0.2 to +0.36 while top heads stay near the LLaVA baseline. Feature-level alignment barely changes MKNN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A contrastive neighborhood objective can induce local cross-modal MKNN alignment in selected heads; pointwise feature matching does not.

record.problems: Alignment-score outcomes are presented in figures without reported uncertainty estimates. The reported alignment changes follow deliberate HeRA training and therefore do not establish natural convergence with model scale or capability.

untested.parts: No comparison of alignment across independently trained models as scale or capability grows; Qwen2.5 3B/7B/14B head maps are shown but no scale trend is stated.
Natural LLM-to-DINOv2 MKNN is plotted per head and layer, but not related to model capability or size; post-training alignment is induced by HeRA.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests.
No cross-model recurrence of interpretable features or circuits.
No variation of the similarity metric, k, or input distribution for measured alignment. Teacher-encoder variation is reported only as downstream VQA scores.
No test of plateau or of shared data or objectives as the cause of natural alignment.

missing.what: Natural (pre-multimodal-training) per-layer and per-head MKNN alignment of text-only Qwen2.5 LLMs with DINOv2-L, on 1,000 GranD captions. Values are figure-only, with the max head around 0.2 and layers far lower. Not a version test but relevant to V6-style granularity dependence.
missing.locator: Fig. 3 left; Fig. 6 left; Fig. 7 left; Sec. 3.3 Heads Selection; App. C.2

missing.what: Base LLM vs LLaVA-trained MKNN for worst and top heads, showing natural rank preservation after multimodal training, plus the competitor-method comparison on Qwen3-8B.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r1–r30 correctly carry versions ['none'] because they measure alignment induced by HeRA. The comparator rows' state 'observed' means 'unchanged from LLaVA', which is ambiguous, but they are unlinked so it is harmless. Qwen2.5 head-alignment plots exist at three sizes, but the authors draw no scale conclusion and report no exact numbers. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure naturally occurring alignment across independently trained models as model size or capability increases.
Measures cross-modal MKNN alignment after alignment is deliberately trained, not whether alignment naturally rises with the capabilities of vision and language models.
No comparison of networks trained from different random initializations.
Does not test mapping, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired interchangeability.
Does not test recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Does not test how convergence varies with similarity metrics, metric settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not test whether naturally observed alignment plateaus or is explained by shared training data or objectives.
